skill.title: Prove De Moivre's Theorem by induction
skill.input: (cos θ + i sin θ)ⁿ, n ∈ N

legend.1: the real bracket, cos kθ cos θ − sin kθ sin θ
legend.2: the imaginary bracket, cos kθ sin θ + sin kθ cos θ
legend.3: the result for k + 1, cos(k+1)θ + i sin(k+1)θ

steps.ask: What does (cos θ + i sin θ) to the power 1 equal, and does it match the right-hand side when n = 1?
steps.title: Test the result for n = 1

lines.text: Let $P(n)$ be the statement $(\cos\theta + i\sin\theta)^n = \cos(n\theta) + i\sin(n\theta)$.
So $P(1)$ is true.

steps.ask: If the statement is true for n = k, what must you show for n = k + 1?
steps.title: Assume the result is true for n = k

lines.text: This is $P(k)$. We now test $P(k+1)$.

steps.ask: How can the power k + 1 be written as the power k times one more factor?
steps.title: Write the (k + 1) power as a product

steps.ask: When you multiply out the brackets, what does i² become, and which terms are real?
steps.title: Multiply out the brackets

lines.text: Replace $i^2$ with $-1$.

steps.ask: Which terms have no i and which have an i? How should they be grouped?
steps.title: Group the real and imaginary parts

steps.ask: Which addition formulas match these two brackets, and what single angle do they give?
steps.title: Use the addition formulas

lines.text: $\cos(A+B) = \cos A\cos B - \sin A\sin B$ and $\sin(A+B) = \sin A\cos B + \cos A\sin B$, with $A = k\theta$ and $B = \theta$.
So $P(k+1)$ is true.

steps.ask: Given that P(1) is true and P(k) implies P(k+1), what does induction let you conclude?
steps.title: State the conclusion

lines.text: $P(1)$ is true. If $P(k)$ is true then $P(k+1)$ is true. Hence $P(n)$ is true for all positive integers $n$.

lesson.note: Changed one thing: the statement uses cos θ − i sin θ, so the imaginary bracket is subtracted. The induction steps are the same, though the grouping sits inside the multiply step.

legend.1: the real bracket, cos kθ cos θ − sin kθ sin θ
legend.2: the imaginary bracket, cos kθ sin θ + sin kθ cos θ
legend.3: the result for k + 1, cos(k+1)θ − i sin(k+1)θ

steps.ask: What does the statement give when n = 1, and does the left side match the right side?
steps.title: Test the result for n = 1

lines.text: Let $P(n)$ be the statement $(\cos\theta - i\sin\theta)^n = \cos n\theta - i\sin n\theta$.
So $P(1)$ is true.

steps.ask: What do you assume for n = k, and what must you then show for k + 1?
steps.title: Assume the result is true for n = k

lines.text: This is $P(k)$. We now test $P(k+1)$.

steps.ask: How can you split the power k + 1 into the power k and one more factor?
steps.title: Write the (k + 1) power as a product

steps.ask: After you multiply out, what does i² equal, and which terms are real?
steps.title: Multiply out the brackets

lines.tex: &= \cos k\theta\cos\theta - i\cos k\theta\sin\theta - i\sin k\theta\cos\theta + i^2\sin k\theta\sin\theta

lines.text: Replace $i^2$ with $-1$ and group the real and imaginary parts.

steps.ask: Which addition formulas turn these brackets into one angle, and what are A and B?
steps.title: Use the addition formulas

lines.text: $\cos(A+B) = \cos A\cos B - \sin A\sin B$ and $\sin(A+B) = \sin A\cos B + \cos A\sin B$, with $A = k\theta$ and $B = \theta$.
So $P(k+1)$ is true.

steps.ask: What three facts together prove the result for every positive integer n?
steps.title: State the conclusion

lines.text: $P(1)$ is true. If $P(k)$ is true then $P(k+1)$ is true. Hence $P(n)$ is true for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

lesson.note: Compared with the previous problem, the sign goes back to plus and a modulus r is added, so every step carries r to the power k + 1. The induction steps are the same.

legend.1: the real bracket, cos kθ cos θ − sin kθ sin θ
legend.2: the imaginary bracket, cos kθ sin θ + sin kθ cos θ
legend.3: the result for k + 1, cos(k+1)θ + i sin(k+1)θ

steps.ask: With n = 1, what does the left side reduce to, and how does it compare with the right side?
steps.title: Test the result for n = 1

lines.text: Let $P(n)$ be the statement $[r(\cos\theta + i\sin\theta)]^n = r^n(\cos n\theta + i\sin n\theta)$.
So $P(1)$ is true.

steps.ask: What is assumed for n = k, and what must be shown for k + 1?
steps.title: Assume the result is true for n = k

lines.text: This is $P(k)$. We now test $P(k+1)$.

steps.ask: How can the power k + 1 be split into the power k times one more copy of the bracket?
steps.title: Write the (k + 1) power as a product

lines.tex: &= r^k(\cos k\theta + i\sin k\theta)\cdot r(\cos\theta + i\sin\theta)

steps.ask: When you multiply out, where does the factor r go, and what does i² become?
steps.title: Multiply out the brackets

lines.tex: &= r^{k+1}[\cos k\theta\cos\theta + i\cos k\theta\sin\theta + i\sin k\theta\cos\theta + i^2\sin k\theta\sin\theta]

lines.text: Replace $i^2$ with $-1$ and group the real and imaginary parts.

lines.tex: &= r^{k+1}\{\hl{1}{[\cos k\theta\cos\theta - \sin k\theta\sin\theta]} + i\hl{2}{[\cos k\theta\sin\theta + \sin k\theta\cos\theta]}\}

steps.ask: Which angle do the cos and sin terms combine to, and what happens to the r factor?
steps.title: Use the addition formulas

lines.text: $\cos(A+B) = \cos A\cos B - \sin A\sin B$ and $\sin(A+B) = \sin A\cos B + \cos A\sin B$, with $A = k\theta$ and $B = \theta$.
So $P(k+1)$ is true.

steps.ask: What three facts together prove the result for all n in N?
steps.title: State the conclusion

lines.text: $P(1)$ is true. If $P(k)$ is true then $P(k+1)$ is true. Hence $P(n)$ is true for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$.
